name: Karbala
tagline: The shrine city of Imam Husayn, heart of Shia pilgrimage
summary: Karbala is where Imam Husayn, grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, was killed in 680, and his golden-domed shrine is one of the most visited places on earth. Pilgrims come all year, and in their millions for Ashura and Arbaeen, when many walk here from Najaf. Check your government's current travel advice for Iraq before planning.
seasonNote: Ashura and Arbaeen follow the Islamic calendar and move about 11 days earlier each year; Arbaeen draws 20 million or more and hotels fill months ahead. Summer passes 48°C, so winter is the comfortable time to visit.
arrival: Many governments advise against some or all travel to Iraq; read yours first. Fly to Najaf (about 80 km) or Baghdad (about 100 km), then take a taxi or shared car. Many nationalities can get a visa online or on arrival, and visas are often waived for Arbaeen pilgrims.
gettingAround: The two shrines and the souks between them are all walkable; vehicles are kept out of the centre. Use taxis or a driver for the desert sights.
cashTip: Iraq runs on cash. Bring clean US dollar notes and change them for dinars; ATMs that take foreign cards are few.
foodTip: Eat where pilgrims eat: kebab and tikka from the grills around the shrines, kahi pastry with geymar cream for breakfast, and the free food (nazri) handed out on holy days.
buyTip: Prayer beads, turbah prayer stones made from Karbala's soil, rosewater, shrine-made textiles and dates.
baseArea: The hotels between the two shrines, along Bayn al-Haramayn and the streets just off it

connections.note: Flights land in Najaf or Baghdad, then about 90 minutes by road.

items.name: Imam Husayn Shrine
items.summary: The golden-domed shrine over the tomb of Imam Husayn, with mirror-tiled halls and courtyards that never empty.
items.expect: Security checks and shoe drops at every gate; women wear an abaya or chador, which can be borrowed. Non-Muslim visitors are usually welcome in the courtyards when dressed modestly.
items.tip: Come before dawn or late at night, when the courtyards are calm and the dome glows.

items.name: Al-Abbas Shrine
items.summary: The shrine of Abbas ibn Ali, Husayn's half-brother and standard-bearer, facing Husayn's shrine across the plaza.
items.expect: The same entry rules as the Husayn shrine; busiest at evening prayers.
items.tip: Its museum of gifts given to the shrine over the centuries is worth an hour.

items.name: Bayn al-Haramayn
items.summary: The wide plaza joining the two shrines, where pilgrims walk back and forth between them.
items.expect: Packed at dusk and on holy days; shaded in parts.
items.tip: Stand in the middle at sunset to see both domes lit at once.

items.name: Tal al-Zaynabiya
items.summary: The small hill beside Husayn's shrine where, by tradition, his sister Zaynab watched the battle.
items.expect: A small shrine room; often crowded with women pilgrims.
items.tip: Pair it with your visit to the Husayn shrine; it is a minute's walk.

items.name: Al-Ukhaidir Fortress
items.summary: A vast 8th-century Abbasid palace-fortress of brick vaults and arches standing alone in the desert.
items.expect: Little shade and few facilities; you need a driver.
items.tip: Go early morning and bring water; combine with Lake Razzaza on the way back.
